lessons.title: Standard Form
lessons.description: Learn standard form for IB Math AA SL: convert numbers, calculate with powers of ten, and check significant figures with worked practice.
keywords: IB Math AA SL standard form
standard form powers of ten IB
lessons.intro: Standard form makes very large and very small quantities easier to compare and calculate. The coefficient must stay in the required range after every operation.
points: Write a non-zero number as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ |a| < 10 and n is an integer. Keep the sign with a for negative values.
When multiplying, multiply coefficients and add powers. When dividing, divide coefficients and subtract powers. Normalize the coefficient at the end.
Use the precision requested by the question. Do not treat every digit on a calculator display as significant.

example.title: Divide quantities in standard form
example.question: Calculate (3.6 × 10⁵) ÷ (1.2 × 10⁻²) and give the result in standard form.
steps: The coefficient 3 is already between 1 and 10.

practice.question: Write 0.0000725 in standard form.
practice.solution: Move the decimal point five places right to get 7.25, so the power is −5: 7.25 × 10⁻⁵.

practice.question: Calculate (4 × 10⁻³)(2.5 × 10⁶).
practice.solution: Multiply coefficients and add exponents: 10 × 10³ = 1 × 10⁴ in standard form.

mistakes: Leaving a coefficient such as 12 outside the required range.
Adding exponents when dividing powers with the same base.
Rounding before completing a multi-step calculation.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Sequences and Series
lessons.description: Find nth terms and sums of arithmetic sequences for IB Math AA SL using the common difference and worked examples.
keywords: IB Math AA SL arithmetic sequences
lessons.intro: An arithmetic sequence changes by the same amount each step. Use the term formula for a position and the series formula when the question asks for a total.
points: The common difference is d = uₙ₊₁ − uₙ. The nth term is uₙ = u₁ + (n − 1)d.
The first n terms sum to Sₙ = n/2[2u₁ + (n − 1)d], or n(u₁ + uₙ)/2 when the last term is known.
Check whether the question asks for a term, a number of terms, or a sum; those are different quantities.

example.title: Find a term and a partial sum
example.question: An arithmetic sequence starts 4, 9, 14, … Find u₁₅ and S₁₅.

practice.question: For 12, 8, 4, … find u₂₀.
An arithmetic series has 18 terms, first term 3 and last term 54. Find its sum.

mistakes: Using n rather than n − 1 in the nth-term formula.
Using the nth-term formula to find a sum.
Dropping a negative common difference when a sequence decreases.

lessons.title: Geometric Sequences and Infinite Sums
lessons.description: Use common ratios, geometric-series formulas, and the convergence condition for IB Math AA SL infinite sums.
keywords: IB Math AA SL geometric sequences
lessons.intro: A geometric sequence changes by a constant multiplier. An infinite geometric sum has a finite value only when its terms shrink quickly enough.
coverage: 1.8 Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
points: The common ratio is r = uₙ₊₁/uₙ. The nth term is uₙ = u₁rⁿ⁻¹.
For r ≠ 1, Sₙ = u₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Equivalent forms are valid when numerator and denominator signs are changed together.
The infinite sum S∞ = u₁/(1 − r) applies only if |r| < 1. State or check this condition before using the formula.

example.title: Find a convergent infinite sum
example.question: Find the sum to infinity of 81 + 27 + 9 + … .

practice.question: For a geometric sequence with u₁ = 5 and r = 2, find u₆.
Does 7 + 3.5 + 1.75 + … converge, and what is its sum?

mistakes: Using the arithmetic formula when the ratio, not the difference, is constant.
Applying S∞ when |r| ≥ 1.
Using the first term as u₀ in a formula that defines the first term as u₁.

lessons.title: Financial Applications of Geometric Sequences
lessons.description: Model compound growth and depreciation for IB Math AA SL with geometric sequences, repeated percentage change, and worked questions.
keywords: IB Math AA SL compound interest
lessons.intro: Repeated percentage changes are geometric because each period acts on the previous balance. Identify the period rate and whether the amount grows or decreases.
coverage: 1.4 Financial applications and geometric sequences and series
points: For compound growth, A = P(1 + i)ⁿ, where i is the rate per period as a decimal and n is the number of periods.
For depreciation by a fixed rate i, A = P(1 − i)ⁿ. The multiplier must match the direction of change.
If deposits or withdrawals repeat, identify whether the question asks for a single future value, a present value, or a sum of payments; do not substitute a one-payment formula for a series.

example.title: Calculate depreciation
example.question: A machine worth ₹12,000 depreciates by 15% each year. Find its value after four years, to the nearest paise.

practice.question: ₹8,000 grows by 3% compound interest for five years. Find the final amount to the nearest rupee.
A value falls from ₹20,000 by 10% each year. What is the multiplier after one year and after n years?
practice.solution: The one-year multiplier is 0.90; after n years the multiplier is 0.9ⁿ, so A = 20,000(0.9)ⁿ.

mistakes: Using 15 instead of 0.15 for a 15% rate.
Using 1 + i for depreciation.
Confusing the number of periods with the initial period index.

lessons.title: Exponents and Logarithms
lessons.description: Apply exponent laws, rational powers, and logarithm laws in IB Math AA SL equations, with domain checks and worked practice.
keywords: IB Math AA SL exponent laws
lessons.intro: Exponent and logarithm laws simplify expressions and turn between multiplicative and additive relationships. Logarithm arguments must remain in their domain.
coverage: 1.5 Integer exponents and introduction to logarithms
1.7 Rational exponents and laws of logarithms
points: For a non-zero base, aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, and (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. A negative exponent means a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
For positive a, a¹/ⁿ is an nth root when defined. A logarithm is the inverse operation: logₐx = y exactly when aʸ = x.
Use logₐ(xy) = logₐx + logₐy and logₐ(xʳ) = r logₐx. For real logarithms require a > 0, a ≠ 1 and each argument x > 0.

example.title: Solve an equation with logarithms
example.question: Solve log₂(x − 1) + log₂(x − 3) = 3.
steps: Solving gives x² − 4x − 5 = 0, so x = 5 or −1. Only x = 5 satisfies the domain.

practice.question: Simplify (x⁵x⁻²)/x for x ≠ 0.
practice.solution: Add and subtract exponents: x⁵⁻²⁻¹ = x².

practice.question: Solve 5ˣ = 17, giving an exact logarithmic expression.
practice.solution: Take logarithms: x = log₅17 = ln(17)/ln(5). The approximate value is about 1.760.

mistakes: Using log(a + b) = log a + log b; there is no such general addition law.
Keeping a logarithmic solution that makes its argument zero or negative.
Applying rational exponent rules without checking whether the real root exists.

lessons.title: Simple Proof and the Binomial Theorem
lessons.description: Build a clear simple proof and expand natural-number powers with the binomial theorem for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL simple proof
lessons.intro: A proof explains why a statement holds across its stated domain. The binomial theorem gives a systematic expansion for a natural-number power.
coverage: 1.9 Binomial theorem for a natural number exponent
points: State the claim and its domain, then use definitions or established results to justify each step. Testing examples can suggest a pattern but cannot prove a universal statement.
In an induction proof, verify the first permitted case, assume the statement for n = k, and use that assumption to prove it for n = k + 1.
The binomial expansion is (a + b)ⁿ = Σᵣ₌₀ⁿ ⁿCᵣaⁿ⁻ʳbʳ. Coefficients follow Pascal’s triangle and the exponents in each term add to n.

example.title: Prove a sum of odd numbers
example.question: Prove that 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n² for positive integers n.
steps: Base case n = 1: the left side is 1 and the right side is 1.
Assume the sum of the first k odd numbers is k².
For k + 1, add the next odd number 2(k + 1) − 1 = 2k + 1: k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)².
example.answer: The statement holds for n = 1 and the induction step is valid, so it holds for every positive integer n.

practice.question: Expand (2x − 1)³.
State the first step needed to prove a statement by induction for all integers n ≥ 4.
practice.solution: Verify the base case n = 4, then assume it for n = k (k ≥ 4) and prove it for k + 1.

mistakes: Assuming the result for n = k + 1 instead of deriving it from the induction hypothesis.
Forgetting to verify the base case.
Using a binomial coefficient with the wrong power of a or b.

lessons.title: Straight Lines and Function Notation
lessons.description: Find gradients and line equations, and interpret function notation, domain, and range for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL straight lines
lessons.intro: A linear rule describes a constant rate of change. Function notation makes the input-output relationship explicit and helps track domain restrictions.
coverage: 2.1 Gradients and equations of straight lines
points: The gradient through (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), provided x₂ ≠ x₁.
A line through (a,b) with gradient m satisfies y − b = m(x − a).
A function assigns one output to every input in its domain. The range contains the outputs that actually occur; it may be smaller than the codomain.

example.title: Find a line through two points
example.question: Find the equation of the line through (2, −1) and (6, 7).

practice.question: Evaluate f(−2) for f(x)=x²−3x.
Find the gradient of the line through (−3,2) and (1,−6).

mistakes: Reversing the order of subtraction in only one part of the gradient formula.
Treating an input outside the domain as a valid function value.

lessons.title: Function Graphs, Features and Intersections
lessons.description: Sketch IB Math AA SL function graphs, identify key features, and solve intersections graphically or analytically.
keywords: IB Math AA SL graph features
IB math graph sketch worked example
lessons.intro: A graph displays how a function behaves. Intercepts, turning points, symmetry and asymptotes can help answer questions and check algebraic solutions.
points: Label axes and important coordinates. A sketch should show the features needed to interpret the function, not just a vague curve.
Roots are x-intercepts; a y-intercept is f(0). A maximum or minimum is a turning value on the stated domain.
An intersection of f and g solves f(x)=g(x). Graphs give useful estimates; algebra can give exact values when the equations allow it.

example.title: Read features and solve an intersection
example.question: For f(x)=x²−4x+1, find its vertex and roots, then solve f(x)=1.
steps: Complete the square: f(x)=(x−2)²−3, so the vertex is (2,−3).
example.answer: Vertex (2,−3); roots 2±√3; intersection solutions x=0 or x=4.

practice.question: For y=−(x−3)²+2, state the vertex and maximum value.
practice.solution: The vertex is (3,2). Since the coefficient is negative, the maximum value is 2.

practice.question: Solve graphically/analytically the intersection x²=2x+3.
practice.solution: x²−2x−3=0=(x−3)(x+1), so x=−1 or 3; these are the intersection x-coordinates.

mistakes: Leaving axes, units or key points unlabeled.
Giving only one intersection when the graphs cross twice.

lessons.title: Composite, Identity and Inverse Functions
lessons.description: Compose functions in the correct order and find inverse functions for IB Math AA SL, with domain checks and examples.
keywords: IB Math AA SL composite functions
lessons.intro: Composition applies one function after another. An inverse reverses a function’s mapping on a domain where each output comes from only one input.
points: (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)); apply g first, then f. In general f∘g and g∘f differ.
The identity function maps x to x. If f has an inverse, f⁻¹(f(x))=x for inputs in the suitable domain.
Find an inverse by setting y=f(x), swapping x and y, and solving for y. A restricted domain may be needed to make a non-one-to-one function invertible.

example.title: Compose and invert linear functions
example.question: Let f(x)=2x+3 and g(x)=x². Find (f∘g)(x) and f⁻¹(x).
steps: For the inverse, y=2x+3; swap x and y, then solve x=2y+3 for y.

practice.question: For f(x)=x−4 and g(x)=3x, find (g∘f)(x).
Find the inverse of h(x)=5x−7.
practice.solution: Set y=5x−7, swap, and solve x=5y−7: h⁻¹(x)=(x+7)/5.

mistakes: Reversing the order in a composite function.
Confusing f⁻¹(x) with 1/f(x).
Finding an inverse without checking one-to-one behavior or the domain.

lessons.title: Quadratic Functions, Equations and Discriminant
lessons.description: Use quadratic forms, the discriminant, equations and inequalities in IB Math AA SL with fully worked examples.
keywords: IB Math AA SL quadratic functions
lessons.intro: Equivalent quadratic forms reveal roots, intercepts or the vertex. The discriminant predicts the number of real roots before solving.
coverage: 2.7 Solving quadratic equations and inequalities; the discriminant
points: Expanded form ax²+bx+c shows the y-intercept; factorized form shows roots; vertex form a(x−h)²+k shows the vertex (h,k).
For ax²+bx+c=0, Δ=b²−4ac: Δ>0 gives two distinct real roots, Δ=0 one repeated real root, and Δ<0 no real roots.
For inequalities, locate critical roots and test intervals or use the parabola’s direction. Include equality endpoints for ≤ or ≥ when they satisfy the equation.

example.title: Solve and interpret a quadratic
example.question: Solve 2x²−3x−2=0 and state the discriminant.
steps: Δ=(−3)²−4(2)(−2)=9+16=25, so there are two distinct real roots.

practice.question: Find the vertex of y=2(x+1)²−5.
How many distinct real roots does 3x²+2x+4=0 have?
practice.solution: Δ=2²−4(3)(4)=−44<0, so there are no real roots.

mistakes: Using b rather than −b in the quadratic formula.
Treating Δ=0 as two distinct roots.
Choosing inequality intervals without checking the sign of the quadratic.

lessons.title: Reciprocal and Rational Functions
lessons.description: Analyze domains, intercepts and asymptotes of reciprocal and rational functions for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL rational functions
lessons.intro: A rational function is a quotient of polynomials. Denominator restrictions shape its domain and may create vertical asymptotes or removable holes.
points: Exclude every input that makes the original denominator zero, even if a factor later cancels.
A zero of the denominator that remains after cancellation usually gives a vertical asymptote; a cancelled factor can create a hole.
For simple rational forms, compare degrees or divide polynomials to identify horizontal or oblique behavior. Check graph behavior with algebra and technology where useful.

example.title: Find domain and asymptotes
example.question: For f(x)=(x+1)/(x−2), state the domain and vertical and horizontal asymptotes.
steps: The denominator is zero at x=2, so exclude x=2.
The numerator is nonzero at x=2, so x=2 is a vertical asymptote.
Numerator and denominator have equal degree and leading coefficient 1, so the horizontal asymptote is y=1.
example.answer: Domain x≠2; vertical asymptote x=2; horizontal asymptote y=1.

practice.question: State the domain restriction for g(x)=1/(x²−9).
For h(x)=(x²−1)/(x−1), what input is excluded from the original function?
practice.solution: x=1 is excluded. For x≠1 the expression simplifies to x+1, so the graph has a hole at (1,2).

mistakes: Restoring a denominator-zero input after cancellation.
Calling every excluded input a vertical asymptote; cancellation can produce a hole.

lessons.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
lessons.description: Compare exponential and logarithmic functions, their domains, inverse relationship and graph features for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL exponential functions
lessons.intro: Exponential and logarithmic functions are inverse families. Their domains, ranges and growth patterns explain how they model changing quantities.
points: For a>0 and a≠1, y=aˣ has domain all real x and range y>0; it passes through (0,1).
The inverse y=logₐx has domain x>0 and range all real values; its graph reflects y=aˣ across y=x.
For a>1 the exponential increases; for 0<a<1 it decreases. A vertical or horizontal shift changes intercepts and asymptotes, so check the transformed equation.

example.title: Solve an exponential equation
example.question: Solve 2ˣ=7 exactly and estimate x to three significant figures.
steps: Divide by ln 2 to obtain x=ln 7/ln 2.
Evaluate the ratio and round only at the end.

practice.question: State the domain and range of y=log₃(x−4).
practice.solution: The argument must be positive, so x>4. The range is all real numbers.

practice.question: Is y=(1/2)ˣ increasing or decreasing?
practice.solution: It is decreasing because its base satisfies 0<1/2<1.

mistakes: Allowing a non-positive input to a real logarithm.
Confusing the domain of an exponential function with the domain of its logarithmic inverse.

lessons.title: Function Transformations
lessons.description: Read horizontal and vertical translations, reflections and stretches from transformed function equations for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL graph transformations
lessons.intro: Transformations connect changes in an equation to changes in its graph. Read inside and outside changes separately to avoid reversing the horizontal direction.
points: y=f(x)+k shifts the graph vertically by k; y=f(x−h) shifts it right by h.
A factor a outside, y=af(x), scales vertical distances by |a| and reflects across the x-axis if a<0.
A factor b inside, y=f(bx), scales horizontal distances by 1/|b| and reflects across the y-axis if b<0. Use a key point to check the direction.

example.title: Describe a transformed parabola
example.question: Describe the transformation from y=x² to y=−2(x−3)²+1.
steps: x−3 shifts the graph 3 units right.
The factor −2 reflects it in the x-axis and stretches it vertically by factor 2.
example.answer: Right 3, reflected in the x-axis, vertical stretch by 2, then up 1; vertex (3,1).

practice.question: State the vertex of y=(x+4)²−2.
How does y=3f(−x) transform y=f(x)?
practice.solution: Reflect in the y-axis, then stretch vertically by factor 3.

mistakes: Reading f(x−h) as a shift left; it shifts right by h.
Ignoring the reflection caused by a negative multiplier.

lessons.title: Geometry and Triangle Applications
lessons.description: Use geometric facts, labeled diagrams, and triangle rules to solve IB Math AA SL applications accurately.
keywords: IB Math AA SL geometry applications
geometry diagrams worked examples IB maths
lessons.intro: Geometry questions often combine a diagram with a theorem or trigonometric relation. Mark known lengths and angles before choosing a method.
points: In a right triangle, match opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse to the chosen angle before using sine, cosine or tangent.
For a non-right triangle, the cosine rule uses two sides and their included angle; the sine rule pairs each side with its opposite angle.
In a model or diagram, label units and identify whether the result is a length, area or angle. Round according to the question, not midway through the work.

example.title: Use the cosine rule
example.question: Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 7 cm, with included angle 60°. Find the third side.
steps: Let c be opposite the 60° angle.
Take the positive square root because c is a length.

practice.question: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. Find its hypotenuse.
In a right triangle, the side opposite θ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13. Find sin θ.

mistakes: Pairing a side with an angle that is not opposite it in the sine rule.
Using the cosine rule with the wrong included angle.
Leaving a geometric result without units.

lessons.title: Circles and Radians
lessons.description: Convert between degrees and radians and calculate arc length and sector area for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: convert degrees to radians IB maths
lessons.intro: A radian measures an angle through the ratio of arc length to radius. Circle formulas for arcs and sectors require the angle in radians.
points: A full turn is 2π radians and 360°, so π radians=180°.
For θ in radians, arc length s=rθ and sector area A=½r²θ.
Keep angle units visible in working. If a question gives degrees, convert before using these formulas.

example.title: Find an arc and sector area
example.question: A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 2.4 radians. Find its arc length and area.

practice.question: Convert 150° to radians.
Find the arc length for r=3 m and θ=π/4.

mistakes: Substituting degrees directly into s=rθ or A=½r²θ.
Using diameter instead of radius.
Giving square units for a length or linear units for an area.

lessons.title: Exact Trigonometric Values and the Ambiguous Sine Rule
lessons.seoTitle: Exact Trig Values and the Sine Rule
lessons.description: Use unit-circle exact values and check both possible angles in the ambiguous case of the IB Math AA SL sine rule.
keywords: IB Math AA SL exact trig values
unit circle exact values AA SL
lessons.intro: The unit circle gives exact trigonometric values and signs. The sine rule can produce two possible angles because supplementary angles have the same sine.
coverage: 3.5 Definitions, exact values and the ambiguous case of the sine rule
points: For standard angles, use the unit circle or reference triangles to retain exact values such as sin 30°=1/2 and cos 60°=1/2.
When sin B is known, B and 180°−B may both be candidates. Use the triangle angle sum to test each one.
An inverse-trig calculator result is usually a principal value; it does not automatically list every geometrically possible angle.

example.title: Check both sine-rule possibilities
example.question: In a triangle, a=10 is opposite A=30°, and b=12 is opposite B. Find the possible values of B.
steps: The principal angle is B≈36.9°; the supplementary angle is 180°−36.9°≈143.1°.
With A=30°, both candidates leave a positive third angle.

practice.question: Give the exact value of cos 150°.
practice.solution: 150° is in quadrant II with reference angle 30°, so cos150°=−√3/2.

practice.question: If sin θ=1/2 and 0°<θ<180°, give all possible θ.

mistakes: Returning only the principal inverse-sine angle.
Accepting a candidate that makes the triangle angle sum at least 180°.
Using a decimal approximation when an exact value is requested.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Identities and Relationships
lessons.description: Use fundamental trigonometric identities to simplify expressions and verify relationships for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL trigonometric identities
sin squared plus cos squared identity
lessons.intro: An identity is true for every value in its domain. Transform one side carefully and note any values that make a denominator zero.
points: The fundamental identity is sin²x+cos²x=1.
Dividing by cos²x gives 1+tan²x=sec²x when cos x≠0; dividing by sin²x gives 1+cot²x=cosec²x when sin x≠0.
To verify an identity, simplify one side using valid identities and algebra. Do not cancel terms across addition as if they were factors.

example.title: Simplify using the fundamental identity
example.question: Simplify (1−cos²x)/sin x where the expression is defined.
steps: Then sin²x/sin x=sin x, provided sin x≠0.

practice.question: Rewrite 1−sin²x in terms of cosine.
Simplify tan x·cos x where cos x≠0.
practice.solution: tan x·cos x=(sin x/cos x)cos x=sin x.

mistakes: Dividing by a trigonometric expression without noting when it is zero.
Treating 1−cos²x as (1−cos x)².
Changing only one side of an identity and calling the result a proof.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Functions and Transformations
lessons.description: Read amplitude, period and shifts from sine, cosine and tangent graphs for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL trig graphs
lessons.intro: The equations of sine, cosine and tangent encode repeated behavior. Identify the scale and shift before sketching or interpreting a graph.
coverage: 3.7 Functions and transformations of sine, cosine and tangent
points: For y=a sin(b(x−c))+d or the cosine form, amplitude is |a|, period is 2π/|b|, horizontal shift is c, and midline is y=d.
A negative a reflects the graph vertically; a negative b reverses its horizontal orientation, though the periodic graph may be represented equivalently with a phase shift.
The tangent graph has period π/|b| and vertical asymptotes; it has no amplitude because it is unbounded.

example.title: Read a cosine transformation
example.question: For y=2cos(3x), state the amplitude and period.
steps: The coefficient outside cosine is 2, so amplitude is |2|=2.

practice.question: State the midline and period of y=−3sin(2x)+4.
What is the period of y=tan(4x)?

mistakes: Using π/|b| for sine or cosine; their period is 2π/|b|.
Calling the vertical shift the amplitude.
Trying to assign a finite amplitude to tangent.

lessons.title: Solving Trigonometric Equations
lessons.description: Solve trigonometric equations exactly or graphically and list every solution in the specified interval for IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL trigonometric equations
lessons.intro: A trigonometric equation may have several solutions in one interval. Use reference angles, symmetry and periodicity to find the complete set.
coverage: 3.8 Solving trigonometric equations graphically and analytically
points: Isolate the trigonometric function and identify its reference angle.
Use quadrant signs and the function’s period to generate all candidates, then retain only values in the requested interval.
A graph or technology can give approximate roots. State exact values when the question and angle allow them.

example.title: Solve a cosine equation on one revolution
example.question: Solve 2cos x=1 for 0≤x<2π.
steps: The reference angle is π/3; cosine is positive in quadrants I and IV.
List the values in the half-open interval.

practice.question: Solve sin x=−1/2 for 0≤x<2π.
practice.solution: The reference angle is π/6; sine is negative in quadrants III and IV, so x=7π/6 or 11π/6.

practice.question: Solve tan x=1 for 0≤x<π.
practice.solution: tan x=1 at reference angle π/4, and tangent’s period is π, so x=π/4.

mistakes: Giving only one root in an interval containing multiple roots.
Including an excluded endpoint or missing a permitted endpoint.
Using degrees for an interval stated in radians.

lessons.title: Sampling and Data Displays
lessons.description: Assess sampling methods and read tables, histograms and cumulative-frequency displays for IB Math AA SL.
lessons.intro: A statistical conclusion depends on how data were selected and displayed. Look for bias in a sample and use the correct scale in a graph.
coverage: 4.2 Presenting data with tables, histograms and cumulative frequency
points: A random sample gives members of a population a known chance of selection; a convenience sample may systematically miss groups.
In a histogram with unequal class widths, frequency density = frequency/class width, so bar area represents frequency.
A cumulative-frequency graph shows the number of observations at or below a value; use it to estimate medians, quartiles and proportions below a threshold.

example.title: Compare histogram bar heights
example.question: A class interval of width 5 has frequency 20. Find its frequency density.
steps: Use frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

practice.question: A histogram class has width 8 and frequency 24. What is its density?
Name one concern with asking only students who use the school library about reading habits.
practice.solution: It is a convenience sample and may over-represent students who already use the library, creating selection bias.

mistakes: Comparing histogram bar heights when class widths differ.
Assuming a large sample is automatically representative.
Reading cumulative frequency as the count above a value.

lessons.title: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
lessons.description: Compare mean, median, range and spread for IB Math AA SL data sets and interpret summaries in context.
keywords: IB Math AA SL mean median standard deviation
lessons.intro: A useful summary describes both a typical value and how much observations vary. The choice depends on the data shape and whether outliers are present.
coverage: 4.3 Measures of central tendency and dispersion
points: The mean uses every value but can move substantially because of an extreme observation; the median is more resistant.
Range is maximum minus minimum. The interquartile range describes the middle half; standard deviation measures spread around the mean.
When comparing groups, state the units and connect the numerical summary to the context. Use the same quartile convention or calculator settings for a fair comparison.

example.title: Summarize a small data set
example.question: For 2, 3, 5, 5, 10 find the mean, median and range.
steps: The sum is 25 across 5 values, so mean=5.
The middle ordered value is 5, so median=5.

practice.question: Find the median and range of 4, 7, 8, 12.
Which is more resistant to a very large outlier: mean or median?
practice.solution: The median is generally more resistant to extreme values.

mistakes: Mixing population and sample standard deviation settings without checking the question.
Reporting a spread measure without its units.
Using a mean alone when a strong outlier makes it unrepresentative.

lessons.title: Correlation and Regression Lines
lessons.description: Interpret correlation, use the correct regression direction, and avoid causal claims in IB Math AA SL statistics.
keywords: IB Math AA SL correlation regression
regression line x on y versus y on x
lessons.intro: Correlation describes association; regression predicts one variable from another. The direction of prediction determines which regression line to use.
coverage: 4.10 Equation of the regression line of x on y
points: A correlation coefficient summarizes the strength and direction of a linear association, not a causal relationship.
The regression of y on x predicts y from x. The regression of x on y predicts x from y; they are not interchangeable.
Avoid extrapolating far beyond the observed data. Interpret the prediction in context and consider whether the relationship is plausibly linear.

example.title: Choose the direction of prediction
example.question: A fitted line for predicting test score y from study hours x is y=3.2x+5. Estimate the score for 10 hours.
steps: The question gives a regression of y on x, matching the requested prediction.
example.answer: Estimated score 37, if 10 hours is within a reasonable range of the observed data.

practice.question: A line predicts x from y. Which variable is the input to substitute when predicting x?
practice.solution: Substitute the known y-value because the line models x as a function of y.

practice.question: A strong correlation is observed between ice-cream sales and swimming incidents. Does this show that ice-cream causes incidents?
practice.solution: No. Correlation alone does not establish causation; temperature or season could affect both.

mistakes: Using the regression line in the wrong direction.
Claiming that correlation proves causation.
Extrapolating without warning beyond the data range.

lessons.title: Probability and Conditional Events
lessons.description: Use diagrams, conditional probability and independence rules to solve IB Math AA SL probability questions.
keywords: IB Math AA SL conditional probability
lessons.intro: Probability diagrams organize combined events. Conditional probability changes the reference group, while independence describes when learning one event does not change another’s probability.
coverage: 4.6 Diagrams, conditional probability, combined and independent events
4.11 Formulae for conditional probabilities and independent events
points: For events A and B, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0.
Independence means P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when defined.
Use a tree, Venn diagram or table to show the event structure. Label conditional branch probabilities after the preceding event has occurred.

example.title: Find a conditional probability
example.question: P(French)=0.6, P(Spanish)=0.4 and P(both)=0.25. Find P(French|Spanish).

practice.question: If P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.4 and A,B are independent, find P(A∩B).
If P(A∩B)=0.18 and P(B)=0.6, find P(A|B).

mistakes: Reversing P(A|B) and P(B|A).
Assuming events are independent because they are different events.
Adding overlapping event probabilities without subtracting the intersection.

lessons.title: Discrete Random Variables and Binomial Distribution
lessons.description: Calculate expected values and binomial probabilities for IB Math AA SL, and check the model assumptions first.
keywords: IB Math AA SL discrete random variables
lessons.intro: A discrete random variable assigns probabilities to countable outcomes. A binomial distribution is appropriate only when its repeated-trial assumptions hold.
points: Probabilities in a discrete distribution sum to 1. The expectation is E(X)=ΣxP(X=x), a long-run average.
A binomial model has a fixed number n of independent trials, two outcomes per trial, and constant success probability p.
For X~B(n,p), P(X=k)=ⁿCₖpᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; the mean is np and variance is np(1−p).

example.title: Find an exact binomial probability
example.question: For X~B(4,0.25), find P(X=2) and the expected value.

practice.question: For X~B(6,0.5), find E(X).
State why a binomial model may fail for sampling without replacement from a very small group.
practice.solution: Trials are dependent and the success probability changes after each selection.

mistakes: Using nCk with k outside 0≤k≤n.
Forgetting the failure factor (1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.
Using a binomial model without checking independence and constant p.

lessons.title: Normal Distribution and Z-Values
lessons.description: Standardize normal variables and interpret probabilities for IB Math AA SL using z-values and calculator notation.
keywords: IB Math AA SL normal distribution
lessons.intro: A normal model is centered at its mean and scaled by its standard deviation. Standardization converts a raw value to a common scale.
points: For X~N(μ,σ²), the mean is μ and the standard deviation is σ; the second parameter in this notation is the variance.
The standardized value is z=(x−μ)/σ. Positive z is above the mean and negative z is below it.
For probabilities, specify the tail or interval. A calculator’s normal CDF uses lower and upper bounds, mean and standard deviation; check which tail the question asks for.

example.title: Standardize a score
example.question: A normal variable has mean 100 and standard deviation 15. Find the z-value for x=130.
example.answer: z=2, so 130 is two standard deviations above the mean.

practice.question: X has mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Find the z-value for 58.
What raw value corresponds to z=1.2 when μ=50 and σ=5?

mistakes: Dividing by variance instead of standard deviation.
Reading the second parameter in N(μ,σ²) as σ when it represents σ².
Calculating the opposite tail from the one requested.

lessons.title: Limits and First Derivatives
lessons.description: Connect limits to instantaneous gradients and apply the power rule for IB Math AA SL derivatives.
keywords: IB Math AA SL limits and derivatives
lessons.intro: A derivative is the limiting gradient of nearby secants. The power rule gives an efficient derivative for a power function.
points: The derivative f′(a) is the limit of [f(a+h)−f(a)]/h as h approaches 0, when that limit exists.
For f(x)=axⁿ, f′(x)=anxⁿ⁻¹. Apply this term by term to a polynomial.
A derivative’s units are output units divided by input units; interpret its value as an instantaneous rate when variables have context.

example.title: Differentiate a polynomial
example.question: Differentiate f(x)=3x⁴−2x²+5 and find f′(1).
steps: Apply the power rule to each non-constant term: f′(x)=12x³−4x.

practice.question: Differentiate 5x³−7x+2.
Find the gradient of y=x² at x=3.

mistakes: Reducing the exponent but forgetting to multiply by the original exponent.
Differentiating a constant as if it had a variable factor.
Confusing average gradient with instantaneous gradient.

lessons.title: Increasing, Decreasing and Stationary Points
lessons.description: Use first and second derivatives to study monotonicity, extrema, inflection points and optimization in IB Math AA SL.
keywords: IB Math AA SL stationary points
lessons.intro: The first derivative describes whether a function rises or falls; the second derivative describes how the gradient changes. Together they help classify critical points.
coverage: 5.8 Maximum, minimum and inflection points; optimization
points: Where f′(x)>0, f is increasing; where f′(x)<0, it is decreasing. Solve f′(x)=0 to find stationary candidates.
At a stationary point, f″(x)<0 indicates a local maximum and f″(x)>0 a local minimum. If f″=0, use sign changes or other evidence.
An inflection point requires a change in concavity. For optimization, define the objective, use constraints to reduce variables, find candidates and check endpoints/domain.

example.title: Classify stationary points
example.question: For f(x)=x³−6x²+9x, find and classify stationary points.
steps: f″(1)=−6 gives a local maximum; f″(3)=6 gives a local minimum.

practice.question: For f(x)=x²−4x, find the stationary point and classify it.
practice.solution: f′=2x−4=0 at x=2; f(2)=−4 and f″=2>0, so (2,−4) is a minimum.

practice.question: If f′ is negative on (0,2) and positive on (2,5), what happens at x=2?
practice.solution: The function changes from decreasing to increasing, so x=2 is a local minimum if f is defined and continuous there.

mistakes: Calling every stationary point a maximum or minimum.
Using f″=0 alone to claim an inflection point.
Ignoring boundary values in an optimization problem on a closed interval.

lessons.title: Tangents, Normals and Derivative Rules
lessons.description: Apply product, chain and quotient rules and find tangent or normal equations for IB Math AA SL curves.
keywords: IB Math AA SL product chain quotient rules
derivative rules worked examples AA SL
lessons.intro: The derivative gives the tangent gradient at a point. More complex functions need product, chain or quotient rules before the line equation can be written.
points: Product rule: (uv)′=u′v+uv′. Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x))=f′(g(x))g′(x). Quotient rule: (u/v)′=(u′v−uv′)/v².
A tangent at (a,f(a)) with gradient m has equation y−f(a)=m(x−a).
A normal is perpendicular to the tangent; if the tangent gradient is m≠0, the normal gradient is −1/m. Handle a horizontal tangent as a vertical normal separately.

example.title: Differentiate and find a tangent
example.question: For y=(x²+1)eˣ, find the tangent at x=0.

practice.question: Differentiate sin(x²) with respect to x.
Find the normal gradient to a tangent with gradient 3.

mistakes: Leaving out the derivative of the inner function in the chain rule.
Using u′v′ for a product.
Using the tangent gradient for the normal.

lessons.title: Kinematics with Derivatives
lessons.description: Connect position, velocity and acceleration using derivatives and distinguish displacement from distance in IB Math AA SL kinematics.
keywords: IB Math AA SL kinematics calculus
lessons.intro: In one-dimensional motion, derivatives connect position, velocity and acceleration. Interpret signs and intervals before calculating total distance.
points: If s(t) is position, v(t)=s′(t) is velocity and a(t)=v′(t)=s″(t) is acceleration.
Displacement from t=a to b is s(b)−s(a), equal to the signed integral of velocity. Distance is the total length traveled and is never negative.
A change in direction can occur when velocity changes sign. Split the time interval at such turning points to calculate total distance.

example.title: Separate displacement and distance
example.question: A particle has s(t)=t³−6t²+9t for 0≤t≤3. Find its displacement and total distance.
steps: v(t)=3t²−12t+9=3(t−1)(t−3), so direction changes at t=1.

practice.question: If s(t)=4t²+2t, find v(t) and a(t).
A particle moves from position 2 to position −5. What are its displacement and distance if it moves directly there?

mistakes: Calling displacement and distance the same quantity.
Forgetting that velocity can be negative while speed is non-negative.
Differentiating position twice when only velocity is requested.

lessons.title: Integration and Area
lessons.description: Find antiderivatives, use substitution, evaluate definite integrals and calculate area for IB Math AA SL calculus.
lessons.intro: An indefinite integral reverses differentiation; a definite integral measures signed accumulation. Geometric area may require changing the sign or subtracting curves.
coverage: 5.10 Indefinite integrals, including inspection and substitution
5.11 Definite integrals and area under and between curves
points: Reverse the power rule: ∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C for n≠−1. Always include C for an indefinite integral.
For substitution, choose an inner expression u and include du; change limits when evaluating a definite integral in u.
A definite integral is signed area. For geometric area, integrate upper minus lower and split at intersections or axis crossings when the order changes.

example.title: Find area between a line and a curve
example.question: Find the area between y=4 and y=x² for 0≤x≤2.
steps: On this interval, 4 is above x².

practice.question: Evaluate ∫(6x²−4)dx.
Evaluate ∫₀¹2x(x²+1)³dx.
practice.solution: Let u=x²+1, du=2x dx, limits 1 to 2. ∫₁²u³du=[u⁴/4]₁²=15/4.

mistakes: Omitting +C from an indefinite integral.
Forgetting to change or back-substitute limits after a substitution.
Treating signed integral as geometric area when the curve is below the axis.
